title: If Only You Would Rend the Heavens
summary: The people's prayer continues with a cry for God to tear open the heavens and come down as he did at Sinai. They confess that even their righteous acts are unclean and that they have not called on him. Then they appeal to him as Father and potter, and end by pointing to their burned temple and ruined cities, asking whether he will stay silent.
story: This chapter is the second half of the lament that began at 63:7. There the people remembered the exodus and asked where the God of Moses had gone. Here they ask him to come back in person, with the same earth-shaking power he showed when he came down on Mount Sinai. The prayer is honest about why he seems absent: the people have sinned, and God has hidden his face. It closes on a question rather than an answer, and the answer arrives in chapter 65, where God responds that he has been holding out his hands all day long. The whole of Isaiah is heading toward new heavens and a new earth, and this is the prayer that asks for it.
historical:
The prayer describes Judah's cities as a wilderness and says the temple where earlier generations praised God has been burned with fire. That matches the destruction carried out by Nebuchadnezzar's forces in 587 or 586 BC, when the Babylonian commander Nebuzaradan burned the house of the LORD (2 Kings 25:9). Scholars who date Isaiah 56 to 66 after the return from exile place this prayer before the second temple was finished around 515 BC, perhaps among those who came back to find Jerusalem still in ruins. Those who read the whole book as Isaiah's prophecy take it as a prayer he composed for the generation that would see the ruin. The prayer shares its mood with Lamentations and with Psalms 74 and 79, which also mourn a destroyed sanctuary.

One detail about numbering: in the Hebrew Bible, the verse English Bibles number 64:1 is the last line of chapter 63, so the Hebrew chapter 64 has eleven verses, each numbered one lower than in English. The words are the same.
cultural:
When the prayer asks God to rend the heavens and make the mountains quake, it reaches back to the theophanies (appearances of God) in Israel's memory: Sinai wrapped in fire, smoke, and trembling (Exodus 19:16-19), and poems like Judges 5:4-5 and Psalm 18:7-15 that picture God coming down in storm. The ancient sky was imagined as a solid expanse, so tearing it open was a vivid way to ask God to break into the world.

The confession in verse 6 uses images from the laws of purity. Unclean was a ritual state that barred a person from worship until cleansing. The garment translated filthy rags is, in Hebrew, a cloth soiled by menstrual blood, which the law treated as ritually unclean (Leviticus 15:19-24). The point is not that bodies are shameful but that even the people's best religious deeds, done in a state of covenant unfaithfulness, cannot make them fit to approach God. The potter image in verse 8 came from everyday life: potters worked wet clay on a wheel in every town, and the picture of God shaping a person from clay goes back to Genesis 2:7.
literary: The chapter is poetry in the form of a communal lament. It moves in clear stages: a plea for God to come (verses 1 to 3), a confession of praise that no god acts like this one (verse 4), a turn to sin and its results (verses 5 to 7), a renewed appeal introduced by But now (verses 8 and 9), and a closing picture of devastation that ends in two unanswered questions (verses 10 to 12). The word all runs through it: all our righteous acts, we all wither, we are all the work of Your hand, we are all Your people. The same people who are all unclean are also all God's. The final question, will You keep silent, deliberately leaves the prayer hanging so that God's reply in chapter 65 can answer it.

outline.t: Come down as you did before
Confession: we have sinned and withered
Appeal to the Father and potter
The ruined cities and the burned temple

doctrines.note: The prayer confesses that sin has made the whole people unclean, that even their righteous acts are compromised, and that iniquity carries them away like wind. Sin is not only individual acts but a condition from which the community cannot rescue itself, which is why the prayer asks how they can be saved.

The potter and clay image confesses that God has the rights of a maker over what he has made. Here that truth is not a threat but the ground of hope: because God formed his people, he is asked to keep working on them rather than throwing them away.

Verse 5 asks how anyone can be saved if they remain in their sins, and the prayer answers only by appealing to God himself. Salvation depends on God coming down and acting, not on the people's achievements, which the confession has just called soiled.

words.note: Qara, to tear or rend. It is the word used for tearing one's clothes in grief. The people ask God to tear open the heavens as a garment is torn, an image of urgent, visible intervention. Mark's Gospel describes the heavens being torn open at Jesus's baptism, using a vivid Greek verb for ripping that many readers hear as an answer to this prayer.

Iddah, a word used only here in the Old Testament, refers to menstrual cloth, which the law treated as ritually unclean. The prayer's language is deliberately shocking: the people's most righteous deeds, offered while their hearts were far from God, are as unfit for his presence as that cloth was for the sanctuary.

Yatsar, to form or shape; its participle means a potter. The same verb describes God forming the man from the dust in Genesis 2:7. Isaiah uses it for God as Israel's maker (for example 45:9-11), and Jeremiah 18 builds a whole sermon on the potter at his wheel. Here it grounds a plea: a potter does not abandon the pot he is still shaping.

Av, father. The Old Testament calls God Father only occasionally, and this prayer does so twice (63:16 and 64:8). The title means God is the source and guardian of his people, responsible for them as a father is for his household. It becomes central in the teaching of Jesus, who taught his disciples to pray to our Father.

christ: The New Testament uses this chapter in two ways. Paul echoes verse 4 in 1 Corinthians 2:9, saying that no eye has seen and no ear heard what God has prepared for those who love him; he applies Isaiah's praise for God's unexpected works to the wisdom of God revealed in the crucified Christ. And Mark's Gospel describes the heavens being torn open as Jesus comes up from the water at his baptism and the Spirit descends on him (Mark 1:10). Many interpreters hear that as a deliberate answer to the prayer of 64:1: God has rent the heavens and come down, not with fire that makes mountains quake, but in his Son. The confession of verse 6, that human righteousness cannot make us clean, also prepares the ground for the New Testament's teaching that righteousness is given as a gift in Christ, though Isaiah is speaking of a covenant people's compromised worship rather than setting out a doctrine of justification.

hard.q: Does verse 6 mean that every good deed people do is worthless to God?
hard.a:
The verse is often quoted to say that all human goodness is filthy in God's sight, and that needs some care. In context the speakers are a covenant people confessing that they have sinned, have stopped calling on God, and have been handed over to their iniquity. Their righteous acts, the religious observances they might point to, cannot cleanse them or earn God's favor while their hearts are turned away. Verse 5 also says that God welcomes those who gladly do right, so the chapter does not say that doing right means nothing to him.

Christian traditions draw on this verse in different ways. Many Protestant readers use it to teach that no human work can be the basis of justification before God, which rests on Christ alone. Catholic and Orthodox readers affirm that salvation is by grace while giving more room to good works done in grace as genuinely pleasing to God. On any reading, the verse is a confession, not an accusation hurled at others: the ones who say our righteous acts are like filthy rags are including themselves.

questions: The people ask God to rend the heavens and come down. What would you most want God to do if he broke into your situation, and what does that show about your hopes?
Verse 6 confesses that even our best deeds can be compromised. Where are you tempted to rely on your religious record rather than on God?
How does the picture of God as potter and yourself as clay feel to you: frightening, comforting, or both? Why?
